items.prose: A share trades at £80.00. A one-year European put struck at £90.00 costs £12.00, and the rate is 4%.
items.question: What must the matching call cost?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Rearrange parity: $c = p + S_0 - K/(1+r)^T$.

byKey.no-discount: You used £90.00 for the strike today. Paid in a year, it is worth $90.00/1.04 = 86.54$.
byKey.swapped: You added the strike and took off the share. The share sits with the put, so it adds to the call.

items.prose: A share trades at £60.00. A one-year European call is struck at £50.00, and the rate is 5%. Three dealers quote it.
items.question: Which quote can stand without an arbitrage?

options.why: You checked against $S_0 - K = 10.00$. The floor discounts the strike: $60.00 - 47.62 = 12.38$.
That is more than the share. Selling the call and buying the share would pay £1.00 with no risk.

feedback.correct: £13.10 lies between the floor £12.38 and the cap £60.00.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the floor $S_0 - K/(1+r)^T$ and the cap $S_0$.

explain.text: The floor is $60.00 - 50.00/1.05 = 12.38$ and the cap is £60.00. Only £13.10 lies between them.

items.prose: An American and a European call on the same share have the same strike and expiry. The share pays no dividend and rates are 3%.
items.question: How do their prices compare?

options.text: The American call costs more, for its extra right
options.why: The extra right is to exercise early, and on a share with no dividend that is never worth using.
An American call has every right the European one has, so it can never cost less.

feedback.correct: Equal: early exercise is never used, so it is worth nothing.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether the American holder would ever use the extra right.

explain.text: Selling always beats exercising, because the call is worth at least $S_0 - K/(1+r)^T > S_0 - K$. So the early-exercise right is worthless and $C = c$.

items.prose: A dealer has sold 2,000 puts, each on one share, with delta $-0.25$.
items.question: How many shares must the dealer sell short to be delta neutral?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out the book's delta first, sign included.

byKey.buy: You have the direction reversed. Short puts gain when the share rises, so the hedge must lose then: sell shares.
byKey.full: You hedged one share per put. Each put moves only a quarter as much as a share.
byKey.rest: You used $1 - 0.25$. The hedge is $2{,}000 \times 0.25$ shares.

explain.text: Each short put has delta $+0.25$, so the book's delta is $2{,}000 \times 0.25 = +500$. Selling 500 shares brings it to 0.

items.prose: A share is at £100.00, the rate is 5%, and the one-year European put struck at £100.00 costs £7.14. A dealer offers the call at £11.00.
items.question: You buy the call and lend £95.24, and sell the put and short the share. What do you make today, with no risk?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the money you take in and take away what you pay.

byKey.parity: That is the call's parity price. The profit is the gap between it and £11.00.
byKey.no-discount: You lent £100.00. To have £100.00 in a year you need lend only £95.24 now.

explain.text: You take in $7.14 + 100.00 = 107.14$ and pay $11.00 + 95.24 = 106.24$: £0.90. At expiry the four positions cancel.

items.prose: One-year European calls on one share: the 90 call at £14.00, the 100 call at £8.00, and the 110 call at £1.50.
items.question: Buy the 90 and 110 calls and sell two 100 calls. How much cash do you take in today?

feedback.correct: £0.50, for a payoff that is never negative.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Two sales in, two purchases out.

byKey.sign: You have the sign reversed. Here the two sales bring in more than the two purchases cost.
byKey.one: You sold only one 100 call. The butterfly sells two.

explain.text: $16.00 - 14.00 - 1.50 = 0.50$. A butterfly pays between 0 and £10.00, so being paid to hold it is an arbitrage. The 100 call is above the average of its neighbours, £7.75.

items.prose: An American put is struck at £50.00 with a year to run, at 4%. The share has fallen to £1.00.
items.question: How much more does exercising now give than the best case for waiting, valued today?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare £49.00 now with £50.00 in a year, discounted.

byKey.undiscounted: You compared £49.00 now with £50.00 in a year without discounting. £50.00 in a year is worth £48.08 today.
byKey.best: That is the best case for waiting. The question asks for the difference.

explain.text: Exercise pays $50.00 - 1.00 = 49.00$ now. Waiting can at best pay £50.00 in a year, worth $50.00/1.04 = 48.08$. Exercising wins by at least £0.92.

items.prose: A trader buys a call and sells a put on the same share, with the same strike and expiry, both European.
items.question: What are the position's gamma and vega?

options.text: Both 0: the position is a forward, with delta exactly 1
Twice a call's: both legs add to them
options.why: You added the legs' Greeks without their signs. The short put carries the opposite gamma and vega.

options.text: The same as a call's: the put only shifts the price
options.why: The short put's gamma and vega cancel the call's exactly.
Neither leg dominates. A call and a put on the same strike have the same gamma and vega.

feedback.correct: By parity, call minus put is the share less cash: no curvature, no vega.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use parity: what is $c - p$?

explain.text: Parity gives $c - p = S_0 - K/(1+r)^T$, a straight line in $S_0$. So the position's delta is 1, and its gamma and vega are 0. A call and a put with the same strike and expiry share their gamma and vega.
